screens.prompt: In E3, return the salary for the ID in D3 with INDEX and MATCH instead of VLOOKUP.

hints.syntax: =INDEX(C2:C6,MATCH(D3,A2:A6,0)) — MATCH finds the row number, INDEX reads that row.
hints.func-index: INDEX is the half that returns the value; it needs the column of salaries and a row number.
hints.func-match: MATCH supplies the row number. It needs the column of IDs and the 0 for an exact match, or the row will be approximate.
hints.no-vlookup: This lesson is about the alternative. VLOOKUP cannot look to the left, which is exactly why INDEX + MATCH exists.
hints.match-exact: The third argument of MATCH must be 0. Anything else is an approximate match, which assumes sorted data.
hints.require-ref: Point the formula at the ID cell and at the table, so it still works when payroll adds a row.
hints.value: Check which column INDEX is reading and which one MATCH is searching — they have to be the same rows.
hints.error: #N/A is the honest error here: MATCH did not find the ID in A2:A6. #REF! means the row number fell outside C2:C6, and #VALUE! usually means MATCH was given a range where a single cell belongs.

docs.explain: MATCH answers one question: on which row does this value appear? Searching E-103 in A2:A6 returns 3, because it is the third row of that range. INDEX answers the other question: what is on row 3 of this column? Reading C2:C6 at position 3 returns 88000, and the two nested together give =INDEX(C2:C6,MATCH(D3,A2:A6,0)) = 88000. The 0 in MATCH is the exact-match flag and it is not optional in practice: omit it and MATCH assumes sorted data, so an ID that is not in the list returns the row before it instead of #N/A. The pair matters because each half can point at any column, so the return column no longer has to sit to the right of the search column.

errors.text: MATCH could not find the value in the search range, usually a stray space or a number-versus-text mismatch.
The row number from MATCH is larger than the range given to INDEX, which happens when the two ranges have different heights.
INDEX was given a range and no row number, or MATCH was called with only two arguments.

docs.atWork: The upgrade to VLOOKUP that every analyst eventually makes: it survives a column being inserted, it reads leftwards, and the two halves are separate formulas you can test one at a time.
docs.outcome: Look up a value without being trapped by column order.
